questions.explain: The chapter's RDS billing anatomy lists five dimensions: compute (50–65%), storage (15–25%), I/O requests (5–20%), data transfer (3–10%), and snapshots/backups (2–8%).
options: Four: compute, storage, licensing, and support
Five: compute, storage, I/O requests, data transfer, and snapshots/backups
Three: compute, storage, and licensing
Six: compute, storage, I/O, transfer, backups, and Multi-AZ surcharge
questions.q: AWS bills RDS across how many cost dimensions, and what are they?

questions.explain: RDS for SQL Server runs on Intel and AMD instance families only; Graviton (r6g, m6g) classes cannot run SQL Server, so any inventory listing Graviton next to SQL Server is a data quality problem.
options: db.r6g.2xlarge — Graviton gives the best price-performance for SQL Server
db.t4g.large — burstable Graviton is recommended for dev SQL Server workloads
db.r5.large — previous generation is required for SQL Server 2019
None — RDS for SQL Server cannot run on Graviton (r6g/m6g); only Intel/AMD families are supported
questions.q: Which of these instance classes can run SQL Server on RDS?

questions.explain: gp2 at $0.115/GB-month costs $117.76 for 1 TB plus per-I/O charges above the 3 IOPS/GB baseline; gp3 at $0.08/GB-month costs $81.92 with 3,000 baseline IOPS included and no per-I/O charges.
options: gp2 is cheaper at $81.92 and includes 3,000 baseline IOPS; gp3 costs $117.76
gp3 costs $81.92 with 3,000 baseline IOPS and no per-I/O charges; gp2 costs $117.76 plus per-I/O charges above baseline
Both cost $117.76; gp3 only adds independently scalable throughput
gp2 costs $94.21 and gp3 costs $81.92; neither charges for I/O
questions.q: For a 1 TB RDS volume, how do gp2 and gp3 compare on monthly storage cost and I/O charges?

questions.explain: On the example db.r6i.2xlarge (SQL Server Standard, License Included), the embedded license is about $0.96/hour of the $1.75/hour rate; BYOL drops the rate to ~$0.96/hour, saving ~$0.79/hour or $577/month per instance — $138,000/year across 20 instances.
options: BYOL saves ~$0.20/hour and only applies to Enterprise Edition
License Included is always cheaper because AWS buys licenses at scale
BYOL saves ~$0.79/hour ($577/month per instance) by removing the embedded license, worth $138,000/year across 20 instances
BYOL is only available on Multi-AZ instances
questions.q: The chapter calls licensing the 70% line item. What does the BYOL vs License-Included comparison show for a db.r6i.2xlarge running SQL Server Standard?

questions.explain: For a db.r6i.xlarge at $0.92/hour (SQL Server Standard, License Included), running 50 hours/week instead of 168 saves about $471/month; the license portion makes start/stop schedules dramatically more valuable for SQL Server than for open-source engines.
options: A db.r6i.xlarge dev instance running 50 hrs/week instead of 168 saves ~$471/month, and the license portion makes this especially valuable for SQL Server
Start/stop saves nothing because the SQL Server license is billed per month regardless
Start/stop only works on Single-AZ instances with gp3 storage
Dev instances should always keep Multi-AZ enabled instead of using start/stop schedules
questions.q: What does the chapter recommend for non-production RDS instances instead of Multi-AZ, and what is the illustrative saving?
